# Is Start & Stop technology good or bad for my car? (Alfa MiTO)

If you're sitting in an Alfa Romeo MiTo Progression with that orange indicator light on your dash, wondering if disabling the feature is a smarter move, you are asking questions many engineers and mechanics debate. The core concern usually revolves around three areas: mechanical wear on the engine internals, the health of the 12V battery system, and whether the fuel savings actually justify the complexity.

### Engine Wear and Mechanical Stress

The fear that frequent starting causes more wear than idling is largely a myth rooted in outdated mechanical intuition. Modern start-stop systems utilize dual-mass flywheels specifically designed to absorb the shock of deceleration and re-acceleration, smoothing out the torque curve during restarts. While there is technically an added load on the starter motor and the engagement mechanism every time the clutch pedal is depressed to restart, this cycle is engineered with a specific lifespan in mind.

In terms of engine oil circulation, modern vehicles typically employ electric oil pumps or have low-pressure systems that can prime the engine quickly enough during a micro-cycle to prevent wear. The friction generated by starting an idling engine versus the friction from running it at idle for a minute are comparable in total energy consumption and thermal stress. Unless you are driving exclusively in stop-and-go traffic where the vehicle never reaches operating temperature, the mechanical degradation is negligible compared to the benefit of not circulating oil through hot components unnecessarily during short pauses.

### Battery Architecture and Life Expectancy

The battery issue is the most critical technical constraint here. Standard lead-acid batteries cannot handle the high discharge currents required for a cold crank repeatedly without significant degradation. That's why manufacturers equip start-stop vehicles with enhanced AGM (Absorbent Glass Mat) or EFB (Enhanced Flooded Battery) units. These chemistries are built to withstand hundreds of thousands of charge cycles, far exceeding the typical drive cycle of a passenger vehicle.

However, this introduces a trade-off: if you remove the car from its intended usage pattern—frequent short trips—the battery may struggle to reach full charge before the next stop, leading to premature failure. The alternator in these cars is often tuned differently; it might not spin up as aggressively at highway speeds because the system assumes frequent stops require more charging than long cruises do. If you disable the feature constantly but drive mostly for short commutes, you risk straining the battery just enough to shorten its lifespan, effectively trading engine wear for electrical strain without gaining mileage.

### The Economics of Fuel Savings

The fuel savings are real but often overhyped in marketing materials. Start-stop technology shines only when the vehicle is stationary for a significant duration. If your average traffic light wait time or bumper-to-bumper crawl lasts less than 30 seconds, the energy consumed by the starter motor and the auxiliary loads (radio, fans) during the restart cycle can actually exceed the fuel saved by idling.

Mathematically, if you drive 15% of your miles in stop-and-go conditions where the engine runs for under a minute at a time, the net fuel savings might be as low as 2-3%. However, in heavy urban congestion with frequent red lights and long queues, that figure can climb to 10-15%. The decision to keep the feature active depends entirely on your driving environment. If you are primarily on highways or rural roads where stop-and-go events are rare, disabling the system is a rational optimization. But if you live in a city grid like London or Milan, keeping it enabled usually yields a net positive return on energy efficiency without compromising drivability.
